question: One of the communications officers for the European Council on Refugees and Exiles (ECRE) has used her platform on LinkedIn to demonise Israel and has called the EU both colonialist and racist.

Her exact words were, ‘What else shall we do for the world to listen to us, see us as humans, define Israel as it is a colonial nazi state and hold it and its allies accountable for all its atrocities and crimes committed against Palestinians for 75 years’? She also said, ‘Many of you appreciated the writings of Franz Fanon who wrote “Violence is a cleansing force.

It frees the native from his inferiority complex and from his despair and inaction; it makes him fearless and restores his self‑respect” in the context of decolonisation. However, many of the so-called leftist scholars and preachers of human rights suddenly wanted decolonisation to stay as a theory and not as a process occurring on the ground – it is time to support decolonisation in real life.’ 1.
What is the Commission’s view of such behaviour?

While we appreciate the work of the ECRE, we find these statements intolerable. How can the dissemination of such information and private opinions under the name of an EU-funded nongovernmental organisation be justified?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.7.2024) The Commission recalls that freedom of expression is a fundamental right enshrined in Article 11 of the Charter of Fundamental Rights of the EU and Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights. Yet, as consistently stated by the European Court of Human Rights, freedom of expression is not an absolute right1.

Publicly inciting to violence or hatred directed against a group of persons or a member of such a group defined by reference to race, colour, religion, descent or national or ethnic origin, as well as the condoning, denial or gross trivialisation of the Holocaust, may represent a criminal offence, in line with the Council Framework Decision on combating racism and xenophobia (2008)2.

The Commission stands firmly against antisemitism3, which is incompatible with EU fundamental values. Antisemitic statements have serious consequences for (potential) beneficiaries of EU funds, as elaborated in the replies to questions E-000073/2023, E-006476/2020, E-001741/2021 and E003176/2022, including on the consequences of breaching obligations under grant agreements.
1 In light of Article 10.2 ECHR, the exercise of freedom of expression may be subject to restrictions which must

be prescribed by law, pursue a legitimate aim and be necessary in a democratic society. See ECHR, judgement of 4 December 2003, Gunduz v Turkey, §40; Judgement of 6 July 2006, Erkaban v Turkey, §56. 2 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32008F0913 3 https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/ALL/?uri=COM:2021:615:FIN&pk_keyword=No2Antisemitism
